headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: ECC can write shared files and use MCP, while kotaemon ingests documents via broad cloud APIs and may act on unverified outputs.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ECC can write to filesystem, use MCP, and has shared session/state files; kotaemon consumes documents and chat transcripts via a web UI. That creates a plausible injection path if ECC outputs are placed into files or prompts kotaemon reads. The pairwise bridge is documented only indirectly, so I choose medium over low.
conditions: IF ECC output is copied into kotaemon prompts or uploaded documents
IF either agent treats file contents as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of ECC-generated files into kotaemon
Use a separate workspace directory for each agent
Add a manual review step before any prompt or document import
Strip instruction-like text from shared artifacts
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: ECC touches git history, security findings, session summaries, and MCP configs, and can write/read the filesystem. Kotaemon handles documents, transcripts, and API keys, and sends content to multiple external model APIs with broad network egress. If they share a workspace or files, sensitive data can flow from ECC into kotaemon and then to third parties, making the blast radius large and potentially irreversible.
conditions: IF both agents can access the same directory or mounted workspace
IF kotaemon is configured to send imported content to a remote model API
mitigations: Place each agent in a separate filesystem root
Remove secrets from any shared documents before import
Restrict kotaemon to local-only models for shared data
Audit and rotate any API keys present in kotaemon inputs
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation at the orchestrator

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ECC has unrestricted filesystem write, modify_git_state, and allowlisted network egress; kotaemon has broad network egress and file-backed app data. Even without explicit git support in kotaemon, overlapping writes to shared files or shared app data can cause conflicts and lost updates. The interaction is plausible in default multi-instance setups, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same workspace or app-data directory
IF ECC modifies git state while kotaemon or its plugins also mutate shared files
mitigations: Assign distinct working directories to each agent
Avoid concurrent edits to the same repository
Pause one agent while the other performs writes
Use git locks or a single-writer workflow
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC produces session summaries, security findings, and documentation artifacts, while kotaemon is a RAG/chat system that can render or act on retrieved content. If kotaemon treats ECC output as authoritative, errors can cascade into incorrect answers or downstream actions. The pairwise pathway is inferred rather than directly evidenced, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF kotaemon ingests ECC-generated summaries or findings as source material
IF downstream users rely on kotaemon output without verification
mitigations: Require citation checks before using ECC outputs in kotaemon
Mark ECC-generated content as untrusted in the UI
Add a human review step for any action based on retrieved content
Limit kotaemon to read-only summarization for ECC artifacts
requires-engineering: add confidence/provenance metadata

E_compliance.rationale: ECC explicitly handles session retention settings, security findings, and git history, while kotaemon handles documents, transcripts, and API keys with external API calls. If regulated or sensitive documents are routed from ECC into kotaemon, retention and residency obligations may diverge. The profiles do not prove a specific jurisdiction mismatch, so I keep this at medium.
conditions: IF regulated documents or secrets are transferred from ECC into kotaemon
IF kotaemon's configured model provider stores or processes data outside required residency
mitigations: Review retention settings in both tools
Exclude PHI/PII from shared workflows
Use local models for regulated content
Document which data classes may cross between agents
requires-engineering: add policy-based routing by data class
